question: Six weeks in, a team must decide whether to keep a Claude-assisted intake summarising arrangement or return to the previous approach. Which comparison best supports that decision?
options: A) How much faster the summaries are produced now than the team managed before the trial.
B) How the summaries compare with the team's own on the criteria agreed before the trial began.
C) Whether the summaries are entirely free of error, since a wrong summary can misdirect a case.
D) Whether participants say they enjoy the new arrangement more than the approach it replaced.
correct_answers: B) How the summaries compare with the team's own on the criteria agreed before the trial began.
explanations: Speed alone answers half the question. Faster summaries that are less accurate would push cost downstream into misdirected cases, which is why speed has to be weighed against the agreed quality criteria.

Correct. The decision is a comparison against the realistic alternative, measured on criteria fixed in advance so the standard cannot drift to fit the result. That is what turns six weeks of experience into an evidenced choice rather than an impression.
A demand for zero errors sets a standard the previous human process never met either. Judged that way every arrangement fails, so the test cannot distinguish a good option from a bad one.
Enjoyment affects adoption and is worth knowing, but people can prefer an arrangement that produces weaker summaries. Preference is a secondary signal, not the basis for keeping it.
